findings.failure_scenario: An inode with zone[8] != 0 (a double-indirect pointer — nothing in this tree writes one today, but the field exists and is decoded by Inode::from_le_bytes off the device) is truncated: node.zone = [0; NR_TZONES] drops the pointer, free_zones_of never looks at index 8, and the zone plus everything it names becomes unreclaimable with the bitmap still marking it in use, with no errno. Every other 'unreachable' state in this module answers EIO on purpose (alloc_inode's ino == 0 || ino > ninodes, Stage::fill's len > MFS_BLOCK_SIZE); this one answers success.

findings.short_summary: Bare first_data_zone - 1 instead of checked_sub
findings.summary: zmap_bit keeps a bare `first_data_zone - 1` and the diff adds a comment arguing why it cannot underflow, instead of using checked_sub — against CLAUDE.md's rule for fs crates and against alloc_zone's own precedent for the identical expression.
findings.failure_scenario: CLAUDE.md requires checked arithmetic in servers/, drivers/, fs/, userland/ because [profile.release] sets overflow-checks = false: the bare form wraps silently in the shipped binary while panicking under cargo test. fs/mfs/src/main.rs:1078 spells the same first_data_zone - 1 as checked_sub(1).ok_or(EIO)? with a comment saying exactly why the bare form is unsafe there. With first_data_zone = 0 this function wraps in the shipped server and panics in mkfs's host tests — the two-profile divergence the rule exists to eliminate. free_zone (new this slice) is now a caller.

findings.short_summary: Stage is freely constructible, unlike Blocks
findings.summary: `Stage` is a freely-constructible unit struct, so its documented "created exactly once in main, and the borrow checker is what keeps it the only one" aliasing guarantee is convention rather than type-enforced — unlike `Blocks`, whose private fields force construction through device().
findings.failure_scenario: Any future edit writing `let mut s2 = Stage;` (a one-word mistake, since the type needs no arguments) obtains a second independent &mut path to static STAGE. `let bytes = s1.fill(..)?;` followed by `s2.fill(..)` has the kernel's safecopy write the buffer while `bytes: &[u8]` is still live — undefined behaviour in the one module whose whole design premise is that &mut self serializes access to the static. Give Stage a private field (struct Stage(());) plus a fn stage() -> Stage constructor, mirroring Blocks/device().

findings.short_summary: trunc-dir denial probe aims a real FS_TRUNC at /etc
findings.summary: The new `trunc-dir` denial probe aims a real FS_TRUNC at /etc, violating CLAUDE.md's rule to "never aim a 'must be refused' probe at a file or block whose accidental write would destroy something" — the slice's own create-exists probe demonstrates the safe pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: If MFS's node.is_dir() guard in do_trunc is ever weakened or reordered, this probe frees /etc's directory zones at boot, destroying /etc/motd, /etc/pattern, /etc/scratch, /etc/holey and /etc/deny in one call — taking fs.selfcheck, fs.read, fs.write, fs.trunc, fs.create, fs.hole and fs.leak down together, so the log says nothing about which check regressed. The code comment concedes this ("destructive, but *loud*"), yet ROOTFS_DENY_PATH was created two probes earlier precisely because "a probe that accidentally succeeded would corrupt no proof but its own". A purpose-built empty directory carries the identical EISDIR proof with zero blast radius.

findings.short_summary: write_inode safety rationale falsified by create()
findings.summary: write_inode's stated safety justification — "every caller has already read this same inode through read_inode, so the block it names was checked there" — is falsified by this branch's own new caller, create(), which writes a freshly allocated inode that was never read.
findings.failure_scenario: create() calls write_inode(blocks, mount, ino, &node) for an ino that came straight out of alloc_inode; no read_inode (and therefore no walk::zone_ok) ever ran on it. The write happens to stay inside the inode table because alloc_inode bounds ino by mount.ninodes and inode_location bounds the block by inode_blocks — but that is a different, unstated chain, and the comment now reads as coverage for a check that no longer holds. This is precisely the "doc comment true when written, falsified by a later task in the same branch" class CLAUDE.md's 5.10b lesson names; a future caller trusting the sentence literally would reintroduce an unchecked device write.

findings.short_summary: alloc_zone doc cites a DoS claim this branch deleted
findings.summary: alloc_zone's doc still directs the reader to do_write "for why that leak is a *reachable* denial of service rather than a benign one" — a claim this very branch deleted from do_write, which now documents the leak as closed.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader following the cross-reference lands on do_write's rewritten comment, which states the opposite ("no client-controlled failure occurs after an allocation"). The two comments now contradict each other in the same file, and the surviving one asserts a live security property that no longer exists — the same falsified-in-branch defect class as the vfs_open_payload_offsets_are_ordered_and_disjoint tripwire the PR description calls out.

findings.short_summary: Test comment denies the boot coverage this branch added
findings.summary: The driving_next_dir_chunk_over_a_three_block_directory_converges_on_the_size test comment still claims "The arm no image reaches — mkfs-mfs never builds a directory past one block — so this is the only thing that will ever run it", which this branch falsified.
findings.failure_scenario: The sibling doc comment on next_dir_chunk itself (walk.rs:138-143) was updated by this branch to say the second iteration is now reached at boot via /full's runtime growth and the fs.dirgrow probe; this test comment, five lines of prose asserting the opposite, was not. A reader deciding whether the multi-block scan has boot coverage gets contradictory answers from the same file — the same defect class as the four other in-branch falsifications the PR description enumerates.

findings.short_summary: Tautological const assert restates the line above it
findings.summary: const _: () = assert!(ROOTFS_LEAK_PROBES >= ROOTFS_IMAGE_BLOCKS as usize) restates the definition written two lines above it (ROOTFS_LEAK_PROBES = ROOTFS_IMAGE_BLOCKS as usize), so it cannot enforce the property its comment claims ("must out-number any free-zone count the image can have").
findings.failure_scenario: The comment reads as a guard on the probe's config-independence, but the only edit it catches is replacing the constant's value; it says nothing about the free-zone count it is supposed to dominate, and it holds identically whether the image leaves 1 free zone or 250. This is the tautological-cap-assert class CLAUDE.md's 5.10a lesson names. The real invariant is checkable where the free-zone count is already known: kernel/build.rs computes free = verify::free_zones(&img) and could assert free < ROOTFS_LEAK_PROBES beside its existing headroom check.

findings.summary: A whole new crate dependency (minixrs-mfs) is added to the kernel purely to name MFS_BLOCK_SIZE in build_rootfs, when build_rootfs already imports from minixrs_kernel_shared::rootfs, which defines ROOTFS_HOLEY_LEN as 2 * BDEV_BLOCK_SIZE.

A one-line `pub const ROOTFS_HOLEY_HOLE: usize = BDEV_BLOCK_SIZE;` beside ROOTFS_HOLEY_LEN in kernel-shared/src/rootfs.rs gives the same value with no new dependency, and keeps the hole size and the file length defined together where the const _ that relates them already lives.

findings.short_summary: trunc_demo flattens errnos to off=0 in its FAIL line
findings.summary: trunc_demo's failure report flattens every negative errno to off=0 via n.max(0) as usize, discarding the one piece of information the FAIL line exists to carry.

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**
- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit instruction-file violation)
- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)

**INSTEAD:**
- Restate the technical requirement
- Ask clarifying questions
- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
- Just start working (actions > words)

## Handling Unclear Feedback

```
IF any item is unclear:
  STOP - do not implement anything yet
  ASK for clarification on unclear items

WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
```

**Example:**
```
your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.

❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
```

## Source-Specific Handling

### From your human partner
- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
- **Still ask** if scope unclear
- **No performative agreement**
- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment

### From External Reviewers
```
BEFORE implementing:
  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?

IF suggestion seems wrong:
  Push back with technical reasoning

IF can't easily verify:
  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"

IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
```

**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"

## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features

```
IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
  grep codebase for actual usage

  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
  IF used: Then implement properly
```

**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."

## Implementation Order

```
FOR multi-item feedback:
  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
  2. Then implement in this order:
     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
  3. Test each fix individually
  4. Verify no regressions
```

## When To Push Back

Push back when:
- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
- Reviewer lacks full context
- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
- Technically incorrect for this stack
- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions

**How to push back:**
- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
- Ask specific questions
- Reference working tests/code
- Involve your human partner if architectural

**If you're uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** Name that tension, then tell your partner about the issue you've seen. They'll appreciate your honesty.

## Acknowledging Correct Feedback

When feedback IS correct:
```
✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]

❌ "You're absolutely right!"
❌ "Great point!"
❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
❌ ANY gratitude expression
```

**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.

**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.

## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback

If you pushed back and were wrong:
```
✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."

❌ Long apology
❌ Defending why you pushed back
❌ Over-explaining
```

State the correction factually and move on.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |

## Real Examples

**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
```

**Technical Verification (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
```

**YAGNI (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
```

**Unclear Item (Good):**
```
your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
```

## GitHub Thread Replies

When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.

All 13 fixed and verified. Changes are in the working tree, uncommitted.

## The four correctness fixes

**`create()`'s inode leak** — split `insert_entry` into `reserve_slot` + `store_entry`, and `create` now reserves the directory slot (including the zone its growth may need) *before* `alloc_inode`. A full image gets a clean `ENOSPC` instead of burning an inode per attempt. Better than the reviewer's suggestion in one respect: the reservation writes the parent inode back before the dirent is spliced, so a failure between the two leaves a legitimately grown directory with one zeroed slot — not a leak at all. `DirSlot` is `Copy` scalars only, so carrying it across `alloc_inode`/`write_inode` respects the `Blocks` borrow discipline.

**`free_zone` and the tail block** — refuses the device's last zone. Since nothing else can clear that bit, the reservation is now structural rather than merely initial, and `alloc_zone` can never hand out the block holding the tail label.

**VFS `O_TRUNC` before `EMFILE`** — descriptor allocated first, closed again if the truncate fails. Both failure directions are now safe.

**`do_trunc` and `zone[8..10]`** — an inode naming a double- or triple-indirect slot is `EIO` rather than silently discarded, matching the `EIO`-on-unreachable-state convention the rest of the module uses.

Plus `zmap_bit`'s `checked_sub`, `Stage(())` + a `stage()` constructor, and the errno-preserving `report_rc` in init.

## Two things worth flagging

**The `trunc-dir` probe needed an image change, not just a retarget.** Every existing directory is load-bearing — `/`, `/etc`, `/bin`, `/full`. So `/etc/deny` moved to `/deny/file`, giving the destructive probe a directory whose only occupant is the other denial probe's target. Blast radius is now this battery and nothing else.

**The reviewer's rationale on the `minixrs-mfs` dependency was wrong.** `cargo tree` shows `minixrs-mkfs-mfs` already depends on `fs/mfs`, so the crate was in the kernel's build graph either way — there was no extra compile. I made the change anyway for the locality argument (`ROOTFS_HOLEY_HOLE` now sits beside `ROOTFS_HOLEY_LEN`, tied by a `const _`), but not for the stated reason.

The whole-branch sweep CLAUDE.md prescribes turned up four more falsified claims the review missed: `book/src/servers/overview.md` documented `insert_entry` and the old `create` ordering, two VFS comments still said `/etc/deny`, and `tests/qemu-boot.expected`'s commentary described the probe aimed at `/etc`. Also replaced the tautological `ROOTFS_LEAK_PROBES` assert with a real one in `kernel/build.rs` against the built image (`free < ROOTFS_LEAK_PROBES`), which is where the free-zone count actually exists.

Review of PR #54 (xhigh) found thirteen items. The four with teeth:

`create` did not have `do_write`'s "no client-controlled failure after an
allocation" invariant, and documented that as a deliberate deferral. It is the
strictly worse half of the defect 5.10a fixed: `alloc_inode` + `write_inode`
ran before `insert_entry`, whose `place_zone` / `dir_append_offset` can still
answer `ENOSPC`, so a loop of `open(path, O_CREAT)` against a full image burned
one of the 128 inodes per attempt — and unlike a leaked zone, which `do_trunc`
hands back, nothing recovers an orphaned inode. `insert_entry` splits into
`reserve_slot` + `store_entry`, and `create` reserves the directory's slot,
growth zone included, before claiming an inode. A reservation that fails has
allocated nothing; one that succeeds leaves the directory a legitimately grown
block larger, which the parent inode names, so it is not a leak either. The
parent inode now reaches the device before the entry does — `alloc_zone` zeroes
what it hands out, so the reserved slot reads back free and a failure in
between is benign. `DirSlot` is `Copy` scalars, so carrying it across the two
block fetches respects `Blocks`' borrow discipline.

`free_zone` accepted the device's last zone, which `write_zone_ok` permits.
`mkfs-mfs` reserves that block for the image's tail label by marking its bitmap
bit, and this function was the only thing that could ever clear it — an inode
naming zone 255 would have handed it back to `alloc_zone`, whose own limit is
`mount.blocks`, and the first write through it would overwrite the label
`tail_probe` and MEM's init check exist to verify. Refused now, so the
reservation is structural rather than merely initial.

`do_trunc` zeroed all ten zone slots but `free_zones_of` reclaims only the
seven direct ones plus the single-indirect chain, so a nonzero double- or
triple-indirect pointer was discarded with its bitmap bit still set: a zone
nothing can reclaim, reported as success. `EIO` now, the answer every other
unreachable state in this module gives.

VFS issued `FS_TRUNC` before `fd::alloc`, so an `open(path, O_RDWR | O_TRUNC)`
against a full descriptor table answered `EMFILE` with the file already
emptied. The descriptor is allocated first and handed back if the truncate
fails, so both directions are safe. Linux orders it the same way.

The rest:

- `zmap_bit` kept a bare `first_data_zone - 1`, against the workspace rule for
  fs crates and against `alloc_zone`'s own spelling of the same expression.
  `free_zone` is a caller as of this slice, where a wrapped base would clear a
  bitmap bit chosen at random.
- `Stage` was a unit struct, so its "created exactly once, the borrow checker

- `ROOTFS_LEAK_PROBES >= ROOTFS_IMAGE_BLOCKS` restated the definition written
